newsitem.title: GERMANY: Arthur Miller's "The Crucible" screens at Berlinale.
newsitem.headline: Arthur Miller's "The Crucible" screens at Berlinale.

text.p: A film version of Arthur Miller's 1953 play "The Crucible" about 17th century Salem witchhunts is as valid a warning of intolerance now as it was when the play was written in the McCarthy era, its director said on Friday.

Nicholas Hytner, whose film had its international premiere at the 47th annual Berlin Film festival, said the dangers of intolerance and suppression of differing views can be seen in countries around the world today, including the United States.

"There is an eternal urgency to what is being said," Hytner said of his film that depicts 17th century witchhunts in Salem, Massachusetts. Miller's play was a thinly disguised rebuke of the anti-Communist hysteria sweeping the U.S. in the 1950s.

"People think it was a long time ago, but since the 50s there has been a rise in the power of religious fundamentalists everywhere," he said. "There are powerful forces even in the United States. It is terribly complacent to say it is over."

He cited extreme interpretations in the United States of "political correctness" as well as fraudulent charges of child abuse levelled against some innocent people as two examples where intolerance and a witchhunt mentality are still apparent.
"Political correctness is virtuous in itself, but it is sometimes turned into an instrument of suppression," said Hytner, a British director who lives in both London and New York.

"The same is true for people wrongly accused of child abuse," he said. "The phrase 'recovered memory' sometimes used (by prosecutors pressing charges of child abuse) will surely look like witchcraft or mumbo jumbo in 25 years time."

"The Crucible" received two Academy Award nominations on Tuesday in Los Angeles -- best screenplay for Miller, who rewrote his play for the film, and best supporting actress for Joan Allen, who plays a wife falsely condemned of witchcraft.

The legendary Miller caused a sensation with the play in 1953 when the anti-communist fervour stirred by Senator Joe McCarthy was at its peak. The play has long since become an American classic, but at the time Hollywood, fearful of McCarthy's attacks, would certainly never have touched it.

"I wish I had a story that someone in Hollywood warned me not to do this film, but I don't," said Hytner. "We just went ahead and made the film." The Hollywood studio 20th Century Fox spent $25 million on it.
Hytner said Miller had no trouble re-writing his play for the cinema, but the director joked: "I felt as if I was asking Shakespeare for amendments to King Lear."

Although the film has drawn critical acclaim in the U.S., it has had a disappointing box office, with less than $8 million so far. Hytner said he wasn't surprised because American audiences have always had a hard time digesting Miller. Hytner expects the film, like Miller's plays, to enjoy greater success outside the United States.

"Arthur Miller has a way of getting under the Americans' skin," Hytner said. "There is a resistance to what he does, holding up a mirror to them. I believe there will be more openness to the film in Europe."
